items.prompt: What is a 1:1's distinctive value?
choices: What surfaces nowhere else, like how someone is really doing
A second place to read project status that the team already sees
A place to assign and track next week's tickets for everyone
items.explanation: Status and assignments already have homes. The 1:1's value is the stuff with no other outlet.

items.prompt: Which item belongs in a 1:1 more than in any other channel?
choices: Sprint planning moving to Tuesdays
A blocker the report has not escalated
Which ticket statuses look stale
items.explanation: An unescalated blocker has no other reliable outlet, so a trusted 1:1 is where it can surface.

items.prompt: Which of these do standup and the tracker already cover?
choices: Feedback someone is holding back
Worry about where their role is heading
Project status
items.explanation: Status is visible in the usual channels. The other two rarely appear there.

items.prompt: A 1:1 spent entirely on project status mainly does what?
choices: Duplicates information that other channels already carry
Breaks a rule about what 1:1s may legally contain
Gives the report extra preparation work between meetings
items.explanation: It is not forbidden, just redundant: the one private regular channel gets used for what is public elsewhere.

items.prompt: Whose time is a 1:1 primarily?
choices: The manager's
The report's
The project sponsor's
items.explanation: The manager has other channels to push information; the report often has none.

items.prompt: Which item is rarely covered anywhere else?
choices: The deadline on Friday afternoon
A team-wide announcement about sprints
Where the person wants to grow
items.explanation: Growth wishes usually wait for a review months away, if they surface at all.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, how many of the report's three real concerns made it into the 1:1?
choices: None
All three
Exactly one
items.explanation: The conversation was all the manager's list, so none of the three came up.

items.prompt: Why did none of the three concerns come up?
choices: The report had nothing real on their mind
Nothing in the structure made space for them
The manager chose to ignore them on purpose
items.explanation: The report did have concerns; the structure never gave them room.

items.prompt: A manager defends their 1:1s as valuable because they covered a deadline, ticket statuses and a schedule change in one sitting. What is the strongest critique?
choices: Four topics is too many for one thirty-minute meeting to cover well
A schedule change belongs in a team meeting, not a private one
Those items all have other homes, so the unique value got no space
Deadlines should be reviewed weekly, not inside a 1:1 slot
items.explanation: Volume is not the measure. Each covered item is visible elsewhere, while nothing with no other outlet was raised.
items.reference:
Where each item already lives
Status, tickets, schedule changes: standup, tracker, announcements
How they are doing, unescalated blockers, feedback, growth: only a trustworthy 1:1
Why: a 1:1 spent on the first row duplicates channels that exist; its distinctive value is the second row.
items.learnMore:
What a 1:1 is for

Every regular meeting competes with other channels for the same information. A 1:1's distinctive value is what has no other reliable outlet.

Common mistake

Judging a 1:1 by how many topics it covered. What counts is whether the items with no other home got space.
items.reflection: Think of a regular meeting you attend. Which of its topics would still reach you if the meeting vanished, and which would be lost?

items.prompt: A team has a daily standup and a shared tracker. A manager proposes dropping 1:1s as redundant. Which reply best holds up?
choices: They rarely carry unescalated blockers or held-back feedback
Standups run too short for status to be reported accurately by each person
Trackers go stale, so the 1:1 should become where all status lives
Dropping the 1:1 would break the company's agreed meeting cadence for managers
items.explanation: The 1:1 is not for status at all. Its worth is the material that those channels do not surface.

choices: The report's list
Neither, it is unstructured
The manager's list
items.explanation: Manager-led means the manager's items come first and the report's get what is left.

items.prompt: In a report-led 1:1, which items come first?
choices: The report's items
The manager's items
The ticket statuses
items.explanation: Report-led puts the report's agenda first so it is protected by construction.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, how many of the 30 minutes were left for the report?
items.explanation: The manager's list took 25 minutes, leaving 5.

items.prompt: What gives the manager's own items another outlet besides the 1:1?
choices: Nothing; the 1:1 is the only one
The report's performance review
Team meetings and written updates
items.explanation: The manager can push information through those channels, so the 1:1 need not carry it first.

items.prompt: Why does the five-minute squeeze keep happening?
choices: The first list gets the time
Reports tend to talk too long
Managers dislike hearing concerns
items.explanation: It is the order that decides who gets protected time, not anyone's intent.

items.prompt: If the report's items go first, what happens to the manager's items?
choices: They are dropped for good
They get covered in the remaining time
They move to the next quarter
items.explanation: In the comparison, the manager's items were fully covered in both versions.

items.prompt: A closing "anything on your end?" after the manager's list is best described as what?
choices: A protected opening
A coaching question
A closing formality
items.explanation: It reads as wrapping up, not as room for something hesitant.

items.prompt: Which kind of item most often has no other outlet?
choices: A concern the report hesitates to escalate
A change to the sprint planning date
An announcement made to the whole team
items.explanation: Hesitant concerns are exactly what other channels fail to carry.

items.prompt: A manager says they always ask what is on the report's mind, but only after covering their own list. Why does that not meet the structural point?
choices: The question should be asked twice, once at the start and again at the close
Their items inherit leftover time, so asking late protects nothing
Asking after the list makes the report feel their time is optional to the manager
Managers should drop their own list entirely and never raise it in a 1:1
items.explanation: The fix is changing which list goes first, not adding the question.
items.reference:
Same 30 minutes, two orders
Manager-led: 25 minutes of manager items, 5 left for the report
Report-led: the report's items first, manager items in the remaining time
Why: whichever list goes first gets protected time; the other inherits leftovers. The manager has other channels, so the report's list goes first.
items.learnMore:
Agenda order is structural

The squeeze is not bad luck. The list that goes first is protected, and the list that goes second takes whatever remains. The manager's items have other outlets; the report's often do not.

Common mistake

Adding an "anything on your end?" at the close and calling that report-led. Asking late is not the same as protecting time.
items.reflection: Think of a meeting where your own item always came last. What would have been different if it had come first?

Their items were covered faster because the report spoke much less overall
Their items were still fully covered; only the order of the meeting changed
items.explanation: Reordering cost the manager's list nothing and gained two concerns that would otherwise not have surfaced.

items.prompt: A report says "fine" in a flat, quiet tone, unlike usual. What should the manager do?
choices: Take it at face value
Gently name what they noticed
Assume they are about to quit
items.explanation: A mismatch between words and delivery calls for a gentle check.

items.prompt: Which two signals does a manager compare?
choices: The date and the time
The speaker and the listener
The words and the delivery
items.explanation: The point is the gap between what is said and how it is said.

items.prompt: Which line is a gentle check?
choices: You seem a bit off today. Is everything okay?
Tell me exactly what is wrong, right now.
Your tone today is not acceptable.
items.explanation: It names the observation lightly and leaves the report in control.

items.prompt: A report always answers in two or three words, and does today with usual energy. What follows?
choices: Press them for more detail
No check-in is needed
Cancel the rest of the meeting
items.explanation: Terse-but-matched is their normal register, not a signal.

items.prompt: Who decides how much to share after a gentle check?
choices: The manager
HR
The report
items.explanation: The manager makes the door visibly open; the report chooses whether to walk through it.

items.prompt: Is noticing a mismatch the same as mind-reading?
choices: No, it is observing a visible gap
Yes, and that is the whole point of it
Yes, and managers should avoid doing it
items.explanation: It rests on observable tone, energy and engagement, not guesses.

items.prompt: What is the manager's job regarding the report's concern?
choices: Force the report to talk
Make the door visibly open
Close the topic quickly
items.explanation: Openness invites; pressure shuts it.

items.prompt: Which is a real mismatch?
choices: Gives a short answer in their usual cheerful tone
Gives a long, detailed answer with energy
Says "great" while disengaged and unusually short
items.explanation: Only the first has words and delivery pointing in different directions.

items.prompt: A usually chatty report says "all good" in two words and looks at the floor. Which next move fits best?
choices: Name the gap lightly, and leave the report room to answer or to decline
Skip the topic and proceed with the agenda to avoid embarrassment
State that they are plainly upset and ask them to explain why
Ask three more detailed questions about their workload and deadlines
items.explanation: The mismatch is real, so a gentle, low-pressure check is warranted.
items.reference:
Words vs. delivery
Words match delivery: take it at face value
Words and delivery disagree (flat, disengaged, unusually short): gently name it
Why: the mismatch between the two signals is the cue, not the brevity of the answer or a hunch about a hidden problem.
items.learnMore:
Listening for what is not said

The words and the way they are delivered are two signals. A real mismatch earns a gentle, low-pressure check; the report decides how much to share.

Common mistake

Treating every short answer as a red flag. A report whose terse answer matches their usual energy is simply being themselves.

items.prompt: Which is a coaching question?
choices: What have you tried so far?
Here is the fix, use backoff.
Why did you not ask me sooner?
items.explanation: A coaching question draws out the report's own thinking before any answer is supplied.

items.prompt: What is the downside of answer-first?
choices: The answer it gives is always wrong in some way
The next similar problem returns to the manager
It takes much longer in the moment than coaching
items.explanation: The report never had to develop an approach, so they come back again.

items.prompt: What does coaching-first cost?
choices: Nothing at all, since it is free
The report's trust in the manager
More time in this conversation
items.explanation: It is slower now, in exchange for a stronger report later.

items.prompt: What does coaching-first build over time?
choices: The report's own problem-solving
The report's dependence on the manager
The length of each meeting
items.explanation: Working it out themselves is how the skill grows.

items.prompt: A report asks what the team's policy on something is. What is the right reply?
choices: Ask them what they think it should be
Give the direct answer
Tell them to look it up themselves
items.explanation: A factual gap is not a problem-solving opportunity.

items.prompt: Which idea from ic-excellence-management does this echo?
choices: Doing the work for them quickly
Avoiding all feedback entirely
Letting someone struggle productively
items.explanation: Both trade quick help for the other person's growth.

items.prompt: Can answer-first ever be correct?
choices: Yes, but it skips building their approach
No, it is always wrong in a 1:1
Only in 1:1s, and never anywhere else
items.explanation: The answer may be right; the cost is what the report did not get to practice.

items.prompt: Which response is the coaching one?
choices: Use exponential backoff.
What would you do next?
Ask another teammate.
items.explanation: It hands the next step back to the report.

items.prompt: A report asks what the on-call swap policy is. The manager replies "what do you think it should be?". What is wrong?
choices: A factual gap got a coaching question, a mismatched tool
Coaching questions should only come after the report has already tried an answer
The manager should have first asked what the report had already read about it
A policy like this is a decision for HR, so the manager should have refused
items.explanation: Coaching suits problems. A missing fact needs the fact.
items.reference:
Two responses to "I'm stuck"
Answer-first: fast now, the next similar problem returns to the manager
Coaching-first: slower now, builds the report's own approach
Factual gap (a policy question): answer directly
Why: coaching builds judgment where the question is a problem to solve; it is the wrong tool where the question is simply missing information.
items.learnMore:
Coaching questions vs. answers

Asking what someone has tried before supplying a fix costs time now and builds their own problem-solving. It suits problems, not factual gaps.

Common mistake

Answering a policy or fact question with a coaching question. That is withholding, not coaching.

It is a cheaper format

items.prompt: In a 90-day quarter, how many 1:1s fit at a 14-day cadence?
items.explanation: 90 divided by 14 is 6.4, and only whole meetings count.

items.prompt: In a 90-day quarter, how many 1:1s fit at a 7-day cadence?
items.explanation: 90 divided by 7 is 12.9, so 12 whole meetings.

items.prompt: In a 90-day quarter, how many 1:1s fit at a 28-day cadence?
items.explanation: 90 divided by 28 is 3.2, so 3 whole meetings.

items.prompt: In a 90-day quarter, how many 1:1s fit at a 56-day cadence?
items.explanation: 90 divided by 56 is 1.6, so 1 whole meeting.

items.prompt: What does each skipped meeting remove?
choices: A status update nobody needed
One of the few moments a concern could surface
Nothing, since status goes elsewhere
items.explanation: The 1:1 is the protected moment, so each skipped one removes an opening.

items.prompt: Where does a report save a real concern if the 1:1 is unreliable?
choices: For the next standup meeting that week
For nobody, because it simply fades away
For a scheduled review months later
items.explanation: Without a dependable slot, concerns wait for the next formal moment.

items.prompt: How does consistency compare with content in importance?
choices: As important as content
Far less important
Irrelevant if the content is strong
items.explanation: A strong meeting nobody can count on is not used for its main purpose.

items.prompt: Meetings move from every 14 days to every 42. What happens to the protected openings in a 90-day quarter?
choices: They fall from 6 to 3
They fall from 7 to 2
They fall from 6 to 4
They fall from 6 to 2
items.explanation: 90 divided by 14 floors to 6; 90 divided by 42 floors to 2.
items.reference:
Protected openings in a 90-day quarter
Every 7 days: 12
Every 14 days: 6
Every 28 days: 3
Every 56 days: 1
Why: openings = floor(90 / days between meetings), and a rescheduled slot signals low priority, so reports save concerns for a review.
items.learnMore:
Consistency is part of the content

Cadence sets how many moments exist for a concern to surface, and cancellations tell the report how much the slot is worth. Both shape whether they use it.

Common mistake

Treating a 1:1 as optional when nothing urgent is pending. The slot is the point, not that week's contents.
items.reflection: Think of a recurring commitment that was often cancelled. How did that change what you were willing to bring to it?

No, it is one case

items.prompt: After a manager reorders the agenda, a report gives guarded one-line answers for three meetings. The manager concludes the structure failed. What is the better reading?
choices: The report is hiding something serious and the manager should confront it
The agenda order was wrong, and the manager should revert to the old one
A long-held habit needs repetition, though the structural fix is immediate
Three meetings is too many, since reports prefer fewer 1:1s
items.explanation: The unit's fourth failure mode: one reordered meeting does not undo an established pattern.
items.reference:
What undoes the structural fix
Structure without mindset: disengaging mid-meeting
Coaching a factual question: answer directly instead
Letting a routine meeting go inconsistent
Expecting one meeting to undo a long pattern: repeat it
Why: agenda order is necessary but not enough; attentiveness, matched tools, a reliable slot and repetition all have to hold.
items.learnMore:
When the structure stops being enough

The 0-to-2 comparison isolates agenda order in one relationship. Genuine presence, the right tool per question, steady cadence and repetition decide whether it holds in others.

Common mistake

Concluding the structure failed after one meeting with a guarded report. Years of a status-check pattern need repetition to reverse.
items.reflection: Think of a change you made that worked once but faded. Which of these four failure modes would have explained it?

items.prompt: A manager reorders the agenda but glances at the clock when the report raises a career worry. Which failure mode is this, and what follows?
choices: Over-applied coaching: the report gets questions instead of answers, and stops asking
Inconsistency: the report expects cancellations, so brings fewer concerns
Structure without mindset: the report notices and stops raising things
None; checking the time is a normal part of any meeting
items.explanation: Order alone does not do the work. The report calibrates to the manager's visible attention.
items.reference:
What undoes the structural fix
Structure without mindset: disengaging mid-meeting
Coaching a factual question: answer directly instead
Letting a routine meeting go inconsistent
Expecting one meeting to undo a long pattern: repeat it
Why: agenda order is necessary but not enough; attentiveness, matched tools, a reliable slot and repetition all have to hold.

items.prompt: Which change to the scenario most limits how far the six-month result transfers?
choices: A newer report with less rapport may open up more slowly than this one did
A manager with more items on their own list than this one had
A report with three concerns rather than two, all about the same topic
A meeting held in a different room and at a new time, with the same people present
items.explanation: The case isolates structure in a relationship with existing rapport. A newer report may need repetition and trust before the same openings are used.
